question: What is the main goal of community mobilisation in Primary Health Care?

options.A: Making people active partners in their own health
options.B: Allowing foreign donors to control local clinics
options.C: Reducing the cost of building government hospitals
options.D: Punishing communities that ignore public health advice

explanation: Community mobilisation shifts people from being passive receivers of care to active participants who help shape health programs. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T4#GNS124_U4_T4_h1)

question: Why do health programs often fail when they are imposed from the outside without community involvement?

options.A: They fail to match cultural realities and local priorities
options.B: Governments never allow outsiders to visit villages
options.C: Local health workers refuse to touch foreign supplies
options.D: They always cost too much money to run

explanation: Interventions that ignore local values and real community needs lack ownership and fail to gain public trust. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T4#GNS124_U4_T4_h1)

question: What does empowerment mean in the context of community mobilisation?

options.A: Building local capacity to solve health problems independently
options.B: Giving financial loans to every household in the village
options.C: Allowing nurses to make all decisions without community input
options.D: Handing out free medicine during festival seasons

explanation: Empowerment equips community members with the skills and confidence to address their own health challenges long-term. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T4#GNS124_U4_T4_h2)

question: Why is transparency critical when mobilising a community for health action?

options.A: It stops villagers from asking questions about disease names
options.B: It guarantees that the federal government will send more funds
options.C: It builds lasting trust between the health team and the public
options.D: It prevents nurses from working long hours at the clinic

explanation: Open communication about goals, resources, and challenges removes suspicion and encourages people to cooperate fully. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T4#GNS124_U4_T4_h2)

question: Which local group is often leveraged in Nigeria to help drive public health campaigns like immunization?

options.A: Traditional rulers and local youth groups

explanation: Traditional and community leaders hold immense influence over public opinion and compliance in Nigerian grassroots settings. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T4#GNS124_U4_T4_h3)

question: A primary health clinic in a rural Nigerian community wants to improve antenatal care attendance. What is the best first step based on local health system realities?

options.A: Report all pregnant women who miss clinic dates to the police
options.B: Consult village development committees and local women leaders
options.C: Close the clinic until pregnant women start coming on their own
options.D: Wait for federal funds to build a brand new modern hospital

explanation: Engaging trusted local structures helps identify why women are not attending and builds culturally acceptable solutions. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T4#GNS124_U4_T4_h3)

question: What is the very first step a nurse should take when entering a new community for health mobilisation?

options.A: Administering vaccines without telling anyone first
options.B: Visiting local leaders to gain entry and approval
options.C: Building a clinic fence using community donations
options.D: Conducting a written examination for all adults

explanation: Community entry respects local hierarchy and customs by seeking permission and blessing from traditional or civic authorities first. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T4#GNS124_U4_T4_h4)

question: Why are methods like drama and town criers often preferred over printed pamphlets for health education?

options.A: Drama groups do not require any planning or preparation time
options.B: They accommodate varying literacy levels and engage local culture
options.C: They are the only communication tools approved by the WHO
options.D: Printed pamphlets are illegal to distribute in rural villages

explanation: Performance arts and verbal community channels ensure that everyone, regardless of reading ability, absorbs the health message. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T4#GNS124_U4_T4_h4)

question: What is one of the key roles of a nurse when acting as a facilitator in community mobilisation?

options.A: Writing laws that fine people who refuse to visit the clinic
options.B: Helping local committees run meetings and prioritize health problems
options.C: Taking over all financial accounts of the local government
options.D: Purchasing private cars for all members of the village council

explanation: As facilitators, nurses guide the process without dominating it, helping residents make their own decisions. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T4#GNS124_U4_T4_h5)

question: How does a nurse act as an advocate for the community within the health system?

options.A: By presenting community needs like clean water and drug supplies to authorities
options.B: By punishing villagers who fail to clean their surroundings
options.C: By replacing traditional healers with certified medical doctors
options.D: By keeping all medical supplies locked away in the clinic store

explanation: Advocacy involves speaking up on behalf of the community to ensure higher authorities provide necessary resources and support. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T4#GNS124_U4_T4_h5)

question: What is a common reason why community members show apathy toward new health programs?

options.A: Excessive amounts of free medicine being supplied
options.B: Past broken promises from government agencies
options.C: Too many nurses wanting to visit the village daily

explanation: Unfulfilled past commitments create cynicism, making residents skeptical of new health initiatives until concrete results are shown. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T4#GNS124_U4_T4_h6)

question: Why is achieving small, quick wins important when dealing with a resistant community?

options.A: It allows the nurse to take an extended holiday leave
options.B: It proves that traditional leaders have no real authority
options.C: It forces the local government to increase health sector taxes
options.D: It helps restore faith and revive interest in the health system

explanation: Tangible, early successes demonstrate competence and genuine commitment, helping to break down skepticism and resistance. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T4#GNS124_U4_T4_h6)

question: Which of the following is an example of a quantitative indicator used to evaluate community mobilisation?

options.B: Feelings of joy among committee members
options.C: Stories told by elders about past epidemics
options.D: The tone of voice used during town hall meetings

explanation: Quantitative indicators involve measurable numbers and statistics, such as vaccination percentages or clinic attendance counts. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T4#GNS124_U4_T4_h7)

question: Why is qualitative feedback just as important as hard numbers when evaluating a health project?

options.A: It takes less time to collect than counting clinic cards
options.B: It guarantees that diseases will never return to the village
options.C: It is required by law for every international aid disbursement
options.D: It reveals whether the community has truly gained ownership and confidence

explanation: Qualitative insights capture people's attitudes, perceived empowerment, and behavioral changes that raw numbers might miss. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T4#GNS124_U4_T4_h7)
